mainTopic: Buying trees in someone else's field: whether the ground comes with them, and how this affects bringing ביכורים and reciting the declaration.
overview: The amud opens by finishing a list of tree names and then gives a second version (איכא דאמרי) of how three tree names are explained. A new משנה follows. According to the תנא קמא, someone who buys two trees in a friend's field does not get the ground under them, while רבי מאיר says he does. The משנה lists what follows: who may trim the trees, who owns new growth, and what happens when the trees die. A buyer of three trees gets the ground, and all those rules flip. The גמרא then quotes a parallel משנה in ביכורים, where the same dispute decides whether the two-tree buyer recites the declaration. שמואל reads that משנה as teaching that רבי מאיר requires ביכורים even from fruit bought in the market, and the גמרא answers three challenges from פסוקים. Then רבה brings a ברייתא in which רבי מאיר says a buyer of one tree does not recite because he owns no land, and שמואל's reading is refuted. The amud ends as רבי שמעון בן אליקים begins a statement to רבי אלעזר, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Finishing the earlier list of tree names
steps.stepSummary: The text completes the earlier explanation of tree names with the word כסיתא, meaning coral trees.
steps.whatsHappening: This one word finishes an explanation the גמרא was giving just before this, matching an old tree name to a familiar one. Nothing new starts here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous discussion was matching names of trees to the names people used in the גמרא's time. This word closes that first version of the list, so the second version in the next step can follow.

keyTerms.meaning: Coral trees, a kind of tree known in the גמרא's time

phrases.english: …coral trees (kasita).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the explanation from the previous daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The last tree name in the first version is identified as כסיתא.

steps.title: A second version of the tree names
steps.stepSummary: Some say the three names are ערונים, ערמונים and אלמוגים, which are laurel, plane and coral trees.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say the three names are ערונים, ערמונים, and אלמוגים. ערונים are laurel trees, ערמונים are plane trees, and אלמוגים are coral trees.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second version of the tree list. It names three trees and says which familiar tree each one is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase איכא דאמרי means another tradition reports the list differently. In this version the names ערונים, ערמונים and אלמוגים are matched one by one to עָרֵי, דּוּלְבֵי and כְּסִיתָא. This finishes the side discussion about trees before the new משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say: introduces a second version of a statement

steps.confusionAlert: This is not an argument or a challenge. It is just a different report of the same list of names.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Aronim, armonim, almugim.
Aronim are laurel trees (arei),
armonim are plane trees (dulevei),
and almugim are coral trees (kasita).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives another tradition of the list just finished.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ערונים are laurel trees, ערמונים are plane trees, and אלמוגים are coral trees.

steps.title: Buying two trees: is the ground included?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that someone who buys two trees in a friend's field does not acquire the ground, while רבי מאיר says he does. It then lists what follows from this.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If someone buys two trees in his friend's field, he has not acquired any ground. רבי מאיר says he has acquired ground. If the trees grow, the field owner may not trim them. What grows out of the trunk belongs to the tree owner, but what grows out of the roots belongs to the owner of the land. If the trees die, the tree owner has no ground.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It asks whether a buyer of only two trees also gets the land they stand on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the תנא קמא, buying two trees gives you only the trees, not the soil. The rules that follow match that view. The field owner cannot trim the branches, because the tree owner has a right to the tree as it is. Shoots from the roots come out of land that still belongs to the field owner, so they are his. Once the trees die, nothing is left for the buyer.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה (written here in short as מַתְנִי׳)
He may trim (cut back the branches)

steps.confusionAlert: The "he" changes from line to line. The one who "may not trim" is the field owner. The one who gets what grows from the trunk ("his") is the tree owner.
steps.whyThisMatters: This dispute about whether two trees bring the ground with them is exactly what the גמרא will connect to the laws of ביכורים.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who buys two trees
in his fellow's field,
has not acquired ground.
Rabbi Meir says: he has acquired ground.
If they grew, he may not trim them.
phrases.notes: The one who may not trim is the field owner, even if the branches shade his field.

phrases.english: And what grows out of the trunk is his;
but what grows out of the roots belongs to the owner of the ground.
And if they died, he has no ground.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַקּוֹנֶה שְׁנֵי אִילָנוֹת בְּתוֹךְ שְׂדֵה חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה, unrelated to the tree-name list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, a buyer of two trees gets no ground. רבי מאיר says he does. Following the תנא קמא: no trimming, trunk growth goes to the tree owner, root growth goes to the land owner, and there is no ground once the trees die.

steps.title: Buying three trees: the ground is included
steps.stepSummary: A buyer of three trees does acquire the ground, so every result from the two-tree case flips.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he bought three trees, he has acquired ground. If they grow, the field owner may trim them. What grows from the trunk and from the roots belongs to the tree owner. If the trees die, he still has the ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה now gives the three-tree case. Here everyone agrees the buyer gets the land, and the משנה lists how that changes each rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Three trees count as buying a real piece of land together with the trees. So the buyer owns the soil, and anything that grows from it, roots included, is his. The field owner may trim branches that spread beyond that area. Even if the trees die, the land itself still belongs to the buyer.
steps.whatToRemember: Two trees: according to the תנא קמא, no ground, and the rules favor the field owner's land. Three trees: ground is included, and everything that grows, plus the land itself, belongs to the buyer.

phrases.english: If he bought three, he has acquired ground.
If they grew, he may trim them.
phrases.notes: Again this is the field owner, who may now cut back the branches.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָעוֹלֶה מִן הַגֶּזַע וּמִן הַשׇּׁרָשִׁין – שֶׁלּוֹ.
phrases.english: And what grows out of the trunk and out of the roots is his.
And if they died, he has ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite case to the two-tree ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three trees bring the ground with them: trimming is allowed, all growth belongs to the buyer, and the ground stays his after the trees die.

steps.title: A parallel משנה about ביכורים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה in ביכורים. There, a buyer of two trees brings ביכורים but does not recite the declaration, while רבי מאיר says he brings and recites.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: We learned in a משנה elsewhere: One who buys two trees in his friend's field brings ביכורים but does not recite the declaration. רבי מאיר says he brings and recites.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by quoting a different משנה with the same dispute about two trees. This sets up a question or discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The declaration over ביכורים speaks of "the land You have given me," which fits only someone who owns the land. The תנא קמא, who holds that two trees bring no ground, says the buyer brings the fruit but cannot recite. רבי מאיר, who holds that he owns ground, says he also recites. The גמרא brings this source to build on next.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned there: quoting a משנה from somewhere else
He brings (the ביכורים, the first fruits)
First fruits brought to the בית המקדש

steps.confusionAlert: Bringing and reciting are two separate parts of the ביכורים מצוה. A person can be obligated to bring the fruit without being allowed to recite.

phrases.english: GEMARA: We learned there:
phrases.notes: This is a משנה in ביכורים (1:6).

phrases.english: One who buys two trees
in that of his fellow,
brings, but does not recite.
phrases.notes: He brings the ביכורים but doesn't say the declaration in דברים 26:1–11.

phrases.english: Rabbi Meir says: he brings and recites.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Connects our משנה's two-tree dispute to the same dispute in ביכורים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In ביכורים: the buyer of two trees brings but does not recite. רבי מאיר says he brings and recites.

steps.title: רבי מאיר obligates even market-bought fruit
steps.stepSummary: שמואל says that רבי מאיר requires ביכורים even from fruit bought in the market.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: רבי מאיר required even someone who buys fruit in the market to bring ביכורים.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה reports a surprising view in the name of שמואל: according to רבי מאיר, even fruit bought in the market must be brought as ביכורים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now we assumed that the argument about two trees depends on whether the buyer owns the ground. שמואל says רבי מאיר goes much further and requires ביכורים even with no land at all. This means owning land is not what makes רבי מאיר obligate.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said:
Rabbi Meir would obligate
phrases.notes: He means obligate to bring ביכורים, the topic of the משנה just quoted.

phrases.english: even one who buys fruit from the market.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how far רבי מאיר's opinion in the ביכורים משנה reaches.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי מאיר, even fruit bought in the market requires ביכורים.

steps.title: Proof from an apparently extra משנה
steps.stepSummary: The proof is that רבי מאיר's ruling in ביכורים would be obvious if it only meant the two-tree buyer who owns land.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know this? Because the משנה teaches something that seems extra. Since רבי מאיר already taught in our משנה that the two-tree buyer owns the ground, it is obvious that he brings ביכורים and recites. So why say it again?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how שמואל knew this, and points to a משנה that seems to say nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In our משנה, רבי מאיר said that buying two trees gives you the ground. Anyone who owns the ground clearly brings and recites, so the ביכורים משנה would be repeating that. A משנה does not repeat for no reason, so it must be teaching something new.

keyTerms.meaning: brings the fruit and recites the declaration

phrases.english: From where do we know this?
From the fact that it teaches an extra mishna:

phrases.aramaic: מִכְּדֵי תְּנָא לֵיהּ דְּיֵשׁ לוֹ קַרְקַע,
phrases.english: after all, he already taught that he has the ground,
phrases.notes: This is רבי מאיר's view in our משנה (step 3), that the two-tree buyer owns the land.

phrases.english: so it is obvious that he brings and recites.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for שמואל's statement.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's claim that רבי מאיר obligates even market-bought fruit.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ביכורים משנה would be repeating something already obvious from our משנה.

steps.title: So רבי מאיר obligates even market fruit
steps.stepSummary: The extra משנה must be teaching that רבי מאיר obligates even fruit bought in the market.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, learn from this that רבי מאיר required even someone who buys fruit in the market to bring ביכורים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the proof: the extra משנה teaches that רבי מאיר requires ביכורים even without owning land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the ביכורים משנה cannot just be repeating our משנה, it must mean that even if the buyer owns no land, רבי מאיר still says he brings and recites. Market-bought fruit is the furthest case of this.
steps.whatToRemember: According to שמואל's reading, רבי מאיר does not make ביכורים depend on owning the land the fruit grew on. רבה challenges this reading in step 15, and step 16 refutes it.

phrases.english: Rather, learn from this:
Rabbi Meir would obligate
even one who buys fruit from the market.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the conclusion from the proof.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to שמואל, רבי מאיר requires ביכורים even from fruit bought in the market. This reading is later refuted in step 16.

steps.title: Challenge: the verse says 'from your land'
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק says ביכורים come 'from your land', which seems to exclude bought fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: 'which you shall bring from your land'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי מאיר's view with a פסוק that seems to require the fruit to grow on your own land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Your land' sounds like land you personally own. Market fruit did not grow on the buyer's land, so how could רבי מאיר require ביכורים from it?

keyTerms.meaning: but it is written! (introduces a challenge from a פסוק)

phrases.english: But isn't it written:
"which you shall bring from your land"!

steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's claim that, according to רבי מאיר, market-bought fruit needs ביכורים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Your land' implies personal ownership of the land.

steps.title: Answer: it excludes outside the Land
steps.stepSummary: 'Your land' means ארץ ישראל, excluding fruit from חוץ לארץ.
steps.simpleTranslation: That פסוק comes to exclude fruit from outside ארץ ישראל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'your land' means ארץ ישראל, not land you personally own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Your land' is read as the land of the Jewish people as a whole. So the פסוק only rules out fruit grown in חוץ לארץ, and says nothing against bought fruit grown in ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: That comes to exclude outside the Land.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Your land' means land you personally own.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Your land' means ארץ ישראל, excluding חוץ לארץ.

steps.title: Challenge: the verse says 'your ground'
steps.stepSummary: Another פסוק says 'your ground', which again sounds like personal ownership.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second פסוק that seems to require the fruit to come from your own ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if 'your land' means ארץ ישראל, the word 'your ground' sounds more personal. That would again exclude fruit you bought.

phrases.english: But isn't it written: "your ground"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge after step 10's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's ruling about market fruit.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Your ground' implies the fruit grew on ground you own.

steps.title: Answer: it excludes a gentile's land
steps.stepSummary: 'Your ground' excludes fruit grown on land owned by a גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: It comes to exclude the land of a גוי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that 'your ground' means Jewish-owned ground, which rules out fruit grown on a גוי's land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Your' is read as 'belonging to a Jew', not 'belonging to you personally'. So fruit grown on any Jew's ground in ארץ ישראל still counts, even if you bought it.

phrases.english: To exclude the land of a gentile.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Your ground' means ground you personally own.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Your ground' excludes a גוי's land, not bought fruit.

steps.title: Challenge: 'which You have given me'
steps.stepSummary: The declaration says 'which You have given me', which a buyer seemingly cannot say.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is written: 'which You have given me'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third פסוק, from the declaration itself, which seems to require that God gave this person the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי מאיר says the buyer even recites the declaration. But a buyer's land was never 'given' to him, so how can he truthfully say these words?

phrases.english: But isn't it written: "which You have given me"!
phrases.notes: דברים 26:10, part of the declaration said when bringing ביכורים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third challenge after step 12's answer.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי מאיר's ruling that the buyer also recites.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The declaration describes land God gave the person, which does not fit a buyer.

steps.title: Answer: You gave me money to buy it
steps.stepSummary: 'Which You have given me' can mean God gave him the money he used to buy the fruit.
steps.simpleTranslation: It means: You gave me money, and I bought the fruit with it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the buyer can say the words, because God gave him the money he used to buy the fruit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'You have given me' do not have to refer to the land. God gave the buyer his money, so the declaration is still true. This answers the challenges from the פסוקים, so שמואל's reading of רבי מאיר survives for now. The next step brings a stronger challenge.
steps.whatToRemember: All three פסוקים can be read in a way that fits שמואל's reading of רבי מאיר: 'your land' means ארץ ישראל, 'your ground' means Jewish-owned, and 'You have given me' can mean the money.

phrases.english: that You gave me money
and I bought with it.

steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Which You have given me' refers to land God gave him.
steps.terutzMaskana: It can refer to money God gave him, which he used to buy the fruit.

steps.title: רבה's objection from רבי מאיר's ruling on buying one tree
steps.stepSummary: רבה quotes a ברייתא where רבי מאיר rules that someone who buys one tree in another person's field brings ביכורים but does not recite, because he owns no land.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה objects: "Someone who buys one tree inside his friend's field brings ביכורים but does not recite the declaration, because he did not buy land. These are the words of רבי מאיר."
steps.whatsHappening: רבה attacks שמואל with a ברייתא that quotes רבי מאיר directly. רבי מאיר says that someone who owns a tree but not the land under it does not recite the declaration.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל said that according to רבי מאיר even a person who buys fruit brings ביכורים and recites. But here רבי מאיר says someone who owns an actual tree still cannot recite, because he does not own land. If owning a tree is not enough to recite, owning only bought fruit is surely not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises an objection, usually from a ברייתא or משנה
He brings ביכורים but does not recite the declaration

steps.confusionAlert: רבי מאיר does not say the tree-owner is exempt from ביכורים. He still brings them. He only skips the declaration (מקרא ביכורים), because the declaration talks about land.

phrases.english: Rabba raises an objection:
phrases.notes: He's pushing back on שמואל's version of רבי מאיר, which the last few steps were defending.

phrases.aramaic: הַקּוֹנֶה אִילָן אֶחָד בְּתוֹךְ שֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ –
phrases.english: One who buys one tree within the field of his fellow
brings ביכורים but does not recite,
because he did not acquire land;
these are the words of רבי מאיר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the wording-based challenges were answered, רבה brings a direct ruling of רבי מאיר that contradicts שמואל.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's claim that according to רבי מאיר a buyer of fruit brings ביכורים and recites
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי מאיר says a tree-owner without land cannot recite. A fruit-buyer owns even less, so he surely cannot recite either.

steps.title: שמואל's position is refuted
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא declares a תיובתא: רבה's objection fully refutes שמואל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends the discussion and says שמואל's position is refuted. No answer is given.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before this, every challenge to שמואל was answered. This time the source is an explicit ruling of רבי מאיר, and there is no way around it. So the claim that רבי מאיר lets a fruit-buyer recite is rejected.

keyTerms.meaning: A conclusive refutation; the position cannot stand

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי מאיר, someone who does not own the land does not recite the ביכורים declaration. This is true even if he owns the tree, and surely if he only bought the fruit. שמואל's reading of רבי מאיר is rejected.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the basic rule for the rest of the topic: reciting the declaration depends on owning the land.

phrases.english: This is a conclusive refutation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes רבה's objection by declaring שמואל refuted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: שמואל's claim about רבי מאיר is refuted. A person without land does not recite the declaration.

steps.title: Introducing רבי שמעון בן אליקים's statement to רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new statement, said by רבי שמעון בן אליקים to רבי אלעזר, connected to the case of buying a tree in someone else's field.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן אליקים said to רבי אלעזר:
steps.whatsHappening: This line is a setup. It tells us who is about to speak, and the actual statement comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case of a person who buys a tree in someone else's field leads into a related discussion. The content of what רבי שמעון בן אליקים said comes right after this line.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who brings a question or statement to רבי אלעזר

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְיָקִים לְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: רבי שמעון בן אליקים said to רבי אלעזר:

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְיָקִים לְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the refutation of שמואל to a new discussion about buying a tree in someone else's field.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introduction only. The content of the statement follows.
